problem: Existing embodied navigation benchmarks treat targets as generic instances and ignore user-specific semantics such as object ownership. Prior personalization work relies on image queries or continuous LLM interaction, and none test memory-based grounding in mapped scenes.
motivation: Home assistant robots must resolve queries like 'find Lily's backpack' from a textual description of who owns what, without repeated user input. The paper argues personalization needs internal memory and not repeated LLM API calls, so it builds a benchmark that isolates this ability.
key_idea: PersONAL is a benchmark with textual scene descriptions of object ownership (bipartite owner-object graphs at three difficulty levels) and two modes: personalized active navigation (PAN) and personalized object grounding (POG) on a pre-built map.
insight: Existing zero-shot ObjectNav methods (VLFM, OneMap) reach only 9.88% and 28.93% SR against 63.54% for humans, so the benchmark is far from saturated. Performance falls from easy to hard as ownership becomes many-to-many, and humans with environment memory reach 86%. In POG, the region-gated method (RPG) beats plain query scoring (16.8 vs 11.9 SR total), showing that using the ownership description to gate the memory map helps. The authors attribute the remaining gap to the open-set detector failing on long captions and to embedding memory being imprecise at grounding.
method: Caption refinement: manually rewrote captions for over 3,000 GOAT-Bench/HM3D objects (about half of the originals were faulty), and added open-set room and floor labels.

Episode personalization: assign owners via a bipartite ownership matrix under Easy (1-to-1), Medium (owners with multiple objects), and Hard (shared objects) constraints; GPT-4.1 generates a scene description and a query is paired with it; 300 episodes manually checked, over 90% correct.
PAN task: ObjectNav-style with a 500-step budget, LoCoBot-like camera at 0.88 m with 79° FOV, discrete actions (forward 0.25 m, turn/look 30°, stop), and success within 1 m of the target.
POG task: pre-explore up to 2,500 steps to build a map, then receive the description and query and output the target coordinate on the map; success within 1 m.
PAN baselines: an LLM extracts the target instance phrase from the description, then VLFM or OneMap search for it with the OWL-ViT2 detector; Random and Human baselines are also reported.
POG map: frontier exploration builds a top-down grid of 1x1 m cells, each storing a frozen BLIP-2 embedding (50x50x768).

RPG (Region-gated Personalized Grounding): GPT-4.1 extracts K 'person owns object in room' phrases; each phrase's cosine similarity to the map gives top-3 NMS peaks, which are dilated into a mask; the query embedding is then scored on the masked map and the argmax is the prediction.

setting.backbone: VLFM and OneMap (zero-shot; OWL-ViT2 detector) with GPT-4.1 for target extraction; RPG uses frozen BLIP-2 + GPT-4.1
setting.action_space: low-level: MOVE_FORWARD 0.25 m, TURN_LEFT/RIGHT 30°, LOOK_UP/DOWN 30°, STOP
setting.simulator: Habitat (HM3D scenes); small real-world test on LoCoBot wx250s
setting.privileged: none (Human w. env. memory baseline sees the map beforehand; POG humans see GLB scene files)

numbers_note: Benchmark paper; the PAN and POG splits are the paper's own (no official split name is given, so 'val' is used). Human and Random rows are omitted as baselines. The text says RPG reaches 25% SR, which is the Easy split, while the table Total is 16.8.
results: On PAN, OneMap is the best baseline with 28.93 SR / 22.00 SPL, well above VLFM (9.88 SR) but far below humans (63.54 SR, or 86.00 with environment memory). On POG, RPG reaches 16.8 total SR versus 11.9 for query scoring, while humans reach 87.0. In a real-office test, RPG localized 5 of 15 queries.
limitations: Only simple zero-shot baselines are tested and no trained or end-to-end agents. The open-set detector fails on long LLM-generated captions and the embedding memory is imprecise.

The benchmark is static: it has no dynamic or changing personal information, no humans in the scene, and no lifelong learning. HM3D lacks bounding boxes, so success is measured by a 1 m distance and not by IoU.
Real-world validation is tiny (15 queries in one office), and ownership descriptions are LLM-generated, with over 90% verified correct on only a 300-episode subset.
